newsitem.title: UK: Protestants march noisily on Catholic church.
newsitem.headline: Protestants march noisily on Catholic church.

text.p: Hundreds of Protestants marched noisily past a Roman Catholic church on Saturday night in a protest that highlighted fresh communal tension since the IRA ended a peace honeymoon one year ago.

Marching behind pipe bands dressed in militaristic regalia, the Protestants sang anti-Catholic songs and taunted hundreds of police ringing a tiny Catholic church in the overwhelmingly Protestant town of Ballymena.

The march, the biggest in a 23-week picket of the church in the suburb of Harryville, underlined a new gulf between the pro-Irish Catholic minority and pro-British Protestant majority since the IRA ended a 17-month ceasefire on February 9.

The IRA broke its ceasefire by bombing London's Canary Wharf business complex in an attack that killed two and launched a new phase in the guerrillas' war to end British rule and reunite the province with the Catholic Irish republic.
The demonstration was directed at the refusal of Catholics in the nearby village of Dunloy to allow a parade last summer by the Protestant and fiercely pro-British Orange order.

Protestants carried British Union Jack flags and placards demanding the right to parade their pro-British sympathies weeks before the official start on March 31 of Northern Ireland's flashpoint marching season by Orange Order members.

Last year's marching season sparked the worst civil unrest for decades when police first banned then, after province-wide Protestant protests, allowed an Orange Order march through a Catholic area of the southern town of Portadown.
The Harryville church has been besieged for 23 weeks in what its priest, Father Eamon Cowan, said was a "denial of human rights that does violence to the rights of God."

It was also condemned by political leaders of Protestant Unionist parties, who want the province to stay British, as playing into the hands of the Catholic-backed Irish Republican Army and denying basic civil liberties.
Sectarian taunts from hundreds of Protestants corralled behind a chain of police vehicles were audible inside the church as several hundreds Catholics attended a brief mass.
"Hatred is a demon. Pray for those afflicted by hatred," Cowan told the congregation drawn from the tiny Catholic minority in Ballymena, which is 96 percent Protestant.
Police allowed Protestant pipe bands to parade past the church as soon as the service was over after day-long negotiations between the two communities.
They were joined by hundreds of Protestants including parents with small children and teenagers armed with firecrackers and fuelled with cans of beer.
Ian Broad, a Dublin Protestant who returned to Ireland after eight years in South Africa, drove the 160 miles (240 km) from the Irish capital to lend moral support to the worshippers.

"I came to register my protest against intimidation. It is deeply disappointing after witnessing the changes in South Africa to come back and find people in Ireland still mired in the quagmire of sectarianism," Broad told Reuters.
Cowan told reporters that the protest surrounding Harryville was about religious liberty. "The whole issue has to do with whether we have freedom in Northern Ireland or not."

The IRA, which draws support from the Catholic minority, said this week that it saw no prospect of renewing its truce until a strong British government emerged after elections due by in May which would invite its Sinn Fein political wing to talks.
